title: Unit 1e - Compilation Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing the Compilation unit for CS 103, presented by Mark Redekopp. Covers the compilation process for C++ programs.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 1e of CS 103, titled Compilation. The unit is presented by Mark Redekopp and covers the process of compiling C++ programs, using the command line, dealing with compiler errors, multifile compilation, header files, and basic debugging techniques.
notes_text: This unit transitions students from using GUI-based compile-and-run buttons to understanding the underlying compilation process using command line tools like g++.

title: Compilation Section Header
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Compilation topic. Introduces the core concept of the unit.
main_text: This is a section header slide with the heading COMPILATION. It marks the beginning of the main content covering how C++ source code is compiled into executable programs using command line tools.
notes_text: This section covers the fundamental compilation workflow: writing source code, invoking the compiler, and running the resulting executable.

title: Compiling and Running
summary: Introduces the need to understand compilation beyond GUI buttons. Students will learn what happens behind the scenes when compiling and running programs.
main_text: Until now, most assignments have allowed you to just click a button to compile AND run your program. But what is happening behind the scenes? What if you did not have these conveniences? This slide motivates learning the manual compilation process by showing that the convenient 'Compile & Run' button and automated check systems (like those showing 'Check 1 passed', 'Check 2 passed', etc.) will no longer always be available. Students need to understand how to compile and run programs from the command line.
notes_text: The slide uses red prohibition symbols over the 'Compile & Run' button and the automated checking interface to emphasize that students must move beyond these conveniences and learn the underlying process.

images.description: A 'Compile & Run' button from an IDE with a red prohibition symbol overlaid, indicating students should not rely on this convenience. Below it, an automated test results panel showing 'Check 1 passed' through 'Check 6 passed' also with a prohibition symbol.

title: Using the Command Line
summary: Introduces the command line interface (terminal) on Linux, explaining its advantages over GUIs and basic capabilities for navigating files and running programs.
main_text: While GUIs are nice, we often have more control when using the command line interface (i.e. the terminal). Linux (the OS used by Codio and in CS 103, 104, etc.) has a rich set of command line utilities. Mac and Windows do too, though Windows uses different names for the utilities. By typing commands, we can: navigate the file system (like you would with Explorer or Finder), start programs (vs. double-clicking an icon), and copy, move, delete, rename files and folders. Documentation often uses the symbols $ or > as a placeholder for the command prompt. Don't type it. If you see: $ ./test, you should just type ./test.
notes_text: The command line provides more precise control over compilation and program execution than GUI tools. Learning to use the terminal is essential for professional software development and is the standard interface used in CS 103 and CS 104 courses via the Codio platform running Linux.

images.description: Three images showing terminal interfaces: a terminal icon with a command prompt symbol, a Linux terminal view showing the prompt 'student@studentVM:~$', and a Codio terminal view showing a welcome message with system information and the prompt.

title: Compilers
summary: Lists available C++ compilers including g++, clang++, XCode, and MS Visual Studio, and introduces the concept of Integrated Development Environments (IDEs).
main_text: Several free and commercial compilers are available for C++ development: g++, clang++, XCode, and MS Visual Studio. Several of these have 'integrated' editors, debuggers and other tools and thus are called IDEs (Integrated Development Environments). An IDE combines a text editor, compiler, debugger, and other tools into a single application, making development more convenient.
notes_text: In CS 103, g++ is the primary compiler used. It is a free, open-source compiler available on Linux systems including the Codio platform. Understanding different compiler options helps students recognize that the compilation concept is universal even if the specific tool varies.

title: Compilation and Execution Process
summary: Illustrates the full compilation and execution pipeline from C++ source code through the g++ compiler to an executable binary that runs on the CPU.
main_text: The compilation and execution process involves three main steps. Step 1: Edit and write code in a C++ source file (e.g., test.cpp) containing code like #include <iostream>, using namespace std, int main() with variable declarations and cout statements. Step 2: Compile and fix compiler errors by running the g++ compiler, which takes the source file along with C++ Standard and other libraries and produces an executable binary image (a file of binary machine code like 1110 0010 0101 1001). The compiler command has three parts: options/flags, input file(s) (source), and output executable name. Common compiler options include: -g to enable debugging, -Wall to show all warnings, and -o <name> to specify the output executable program name. The full command is: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test. Step 3: Load and run the executable program by typing ./test. The executable is loaded into memory (RAM) and executed by the CPU.
notes_text: This is a critical slide showing the end-to-end workflow. The dollar sign ($) represents the command prompt and should not be typed. The ./ prefix before the executable name tells the shell to look in the current directory for the program. The compiler translates human-readable C++ into machine-readable binary instructions.

images.description: A flowchart showing the compilation pipeline: C++ source file (test.cpp) flows into the g++ compiler along with C++ Standard Libraries, producing an executable binary image of machine code, which then flows to a CPU/RAM diagram for loading and execution. Below, a detailed breakdown of the g++ command showing options, input files, and output executable name components.

title: Just Know This! - The g++ Command
summary: Emphasizes the essential g++ command students must memorize, breaking down each component: options/flags, input source files, and output executable name.
main_text: This slide highlights the critical g++ command that students must memorize: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test. The command is broken into labeled components: the $ is a placeholder from the command prompt (don't actually type this), g++ is the compiler invocation, -g -Wall are options (aka flags) that enable debugging and warnings, test.cpp is the input file(s) (source), -o is the flag to specify output name, and test is the output executable name (can be anything but usually the base name of the .cpp file). Pro tip: Never type this command more than once per session. The terminal saves your commands. Type the Up-Arrow to cycle through previous commands!
notes_text: This is marked with star icons to indicate it is must-know material. Students frequently lose points or waste time by not knowing this command. The up-arrow shortcut for command history is a valuable time-saver during development.

images.description: An annotated diagram of the g++ command with arrows pointing from labels to each part of the command: Options/Flags pointing to '-g -Wall', Input file(s) pointing to 'test.cpp', Output executable name pointing to 'test', and Command prompt pointing to '$'. Star icons frame the title to emphasize importance.

title: Compiling with g++
summary: Details g++ usage including basic invocation, common options (-o, -g, -Wall), default executable naming (a.out), and how to run the compiled program.
main_text: Most basic usage of g++ is simply: g++ cpp_filenames. This creates an executable using the default name a.out. Common options include: -o to specify the output executable name (other than default a.out), -g to include info needed by debuggers like gdb and kdbg, and -Wall to show all warnings. The most common usage form is: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test. Without the -o option, you can run the default executable with: $ ./a.out. To run the program, precede the executable name with ./ which specifies the local directory. Use whatever executable name you gave to g++ via the -o option. Example terminal session: $ g++ test.cpp creates an implicit output with program name a.out, run with $ ./a.out. With options: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test, then run with $ ./test.
notes_text: The ./ prefix is necessary because the current directory is typically not in the system PATH for security reasons. Without -o, the default output name is always a.out regardless of the source file name. The -g flag should always be used during development as it enables debugger support with no runtime cost.

images.description: Two terminal windows showing compilation examples: one showing basic g++ usage producing a.out, and another showing the full command with -g -Wall flags and -o option followed by running the executable with ./test.

title: Dealing with Compile Errors
summary: Explains the difference between compiler errors and runtime errors, and provides practical tips for solving compiler errors using line numbers and error messages.
main_text: Compiler errors are a good kind of error (or at least better than runtime errors). The compiler GIVES you a line number and error message to help you. Runtime errors usually just produce the wrong outputs or crash, leaving no clues as to why (harder to debug). Tips for solving compiler errors: Find the line number, look at your code on that line, and read the error message carefully. Do an Internet search of key words from the error message (leave out any specific names in the error message) to see if there is an explanation online. Deal with the FIRST error by scrolling to the top of the error messages. If there is too much output, use I/O redirection (more to come), for example: $ g++ -g prog.cpp -o ./prog >& errors.txt and then view errors.txt.
notes_text: A common beginner mistake is trying to fix errors from the bottom of the output. Always start with the first error because later errors are often cascading consequences of the first one. Fixing the first error and recompiling often eliminates many subsequent errors.

title: An Example of Compiler Errors
summary: Shows a concrete example of C++ code with multiple errors and the corresponding compiler error output, demonstrating how to read and interpret error messages.
main_text: This slide presents a side-by-side example of buggy C++ code and the resulting compiler error messages. The source code (errors.cpp) contains: #include <iostream>, int main() with declarations int a, b, c and void* ptr, then attempts cout << bc (undeclared), *ptr = a (void pointer dereference), and return "0" (string instead of int). Compiling with g++ -Wall errors.cpp produces several errors: 'cout' was not declared in this scope (missing 'using namespace std'), did you mean 'std::cout'; 'bc' was not declared in this scope, did you mean 'c'; 'void*' is not a pointer-to-object type; invalid conversion from 'const char*' to 'int' for return "0". It also shows warnings: unused variable 'b' and unused variable 'c' from the -Wall flag.
notes_text: This example demonstrates multiple common beginner mistakes: forgetting 'using namespace std', typos in variable names, misusing void pointers, and returning the wrong type. The compiler output shows file name, line number, and column number for each error, making it possible to locate the exact position of each problem.

images.description: Left side shows C++ source code with line numbers 1-9 containing multiple intentional errors. Right side shows the terminal output from compiling with g++ -Wall, displaying multiple error messages with file names, line numbers, and descriptions highlighted in different colors.
labels: error: 'void*' is not a pointer-to-object type

title: Multifile Compilation Section Header
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of content on multifile compilation, covering how to split and compile C++ programs across multiple source files.
main_text: This is a section header slide with the heading MULTIFILE COMPILATION. It introduces the topic of splitting C++ programs across multiple source files and compiling them together, which is standard practice in real-world software development.
notes_text: Multifile compilation is essential for organizing larger programs. This section covers splitting code across .cpp files, the role of function prototypes, header files, and how to compile multiple files together.

title: Splitting over Multiple .cpp Files - Introduction
summary: Introduces splitting source code across multiple .cpp files, showing a single-file program being divided into split-main.cpp and split-sum.cpp.
main_text: Most real-world software applications have their source code split over multiple files as the code grows. This slide shows an example of a single-file program that contains a sum() function and main() being split into two files. The original single file contains: #include <iostream>, using namespace std, a function prototype int sum(int a[], int n), the main() function that creates an array {4,5,6} and calls sum(array, 3), and the sum() function definition that iterates through the array accumulating values. When split, split-main.cpp contains the #include, using namespace std, and the main() function with a comment noting there is no prototype for sum(). split-sum.cpp contains just the sum() function definition. The question raised is: how does the compiler know if the call to sum() in split-main.cpp is a valid function call when sum() is defined in a different file?
notes_text: This example sets up the problem that function prototypes and header files will solve. Without a prototype in split-main.cpp, the compiler cannot verify that the function call sum(array, 3) is valid since it only sees one file at a time.

images.description: Three code blocks showing the transformation: a single complete program on the left with red arrows pointing to two separate files on the right - split-main.cpp (containing main and the includes but no sum prototype) and split-sum.cpp (containing the sum function definition).
labels: // how does compiler know if this is a valid func. call

title: Splitting over Multiple .cpp Files - Both Files Needed
summary: Emphasizes that when code is split across files, both files are needed to create a complete program; one file alone is insufficient.
main_text: The code to the right is split over two files: main() in one file (split-main.cpp) which declares an array, and a function sum() in another file (split-sum.cpp) which sums the array. But we need BOTH files to create a full program; ONE file alone is not enough to build the entire program. The split-main.cpp file contains #include <iostream>, using namespace std, and int main() which creates an array {4,5,6}, calls int val = sum(array, 3), outputs the value, and returns 0. The split-sum.cpp file contains the int sum(int a[], int n) function that uses a for loop to accumulate array values and returns the sum.
notes_text: This reinforces that splitting code requires all pieces to be present at link time. The compiler needs to see all source files together to produce a working executable. This concept is fundamental to understanding how larger software projects are organized.

images.description: Two code blocks showing split-main.cpp with the main function and split-sum.cpp with the sum function, illustrating that both are required to build the complete program.

title: Splitting over Multiple .cpp Files - Compiler Fact 1
summary: Explains that the compiler only examines one file at a time, requiring function prototypes for cross-file function calls, or a compile error results.
main_text: Compiler Fact 1: The compiler only examines one file at a time. We want functions defined in one file to be able to be called in another. How does the compiler know if the function exists? It doesn't... it only checks when the linker runs (last step in compilation). When translating a single file, the compiler uses/requires a function prototype to verify and know the types of the argument(s) and return value. Without a prototype, a compile-error is generated. The slide demonstrates this with the error output from compiling split-main.cpp alone: $ g++ -g -Wall split-main.cpp produces the error: split-main.cpp:8:13: error: 'sum' was not declared in this scope on the line int val = sum(array, 3).
notes_text: This is a fundamental concept: the compiler processes files independently. It relies on prototypes to validate function calls during compilation of each individual file. The actual function definitions are matched later during the linking phase. This separation is what makes header files necessary.

images.description: Code blocks showing split-main.cpp (with comment highlighting no prototype for sum) and split-sum.cpp, plus a terminal window showing the compiler error 'sum was not declared in this scope' when compiling split-main.cpp alone.
labels: error: 'sum' was not declared in this scope

title: Compiling Multiple .cpp Files
summary: Shows how adding a function prototype enables multifile compilation, and explains that ALL source files must be listed in the g++ command.
main_text: The compiler uses the prototype to check if the right number and type of arguments are being passed and what the return type is. The compiler 'trusts' that if there is a matching prototype, then somewhere and sometime later it will find the definition of that function in some other file (if not in this one). Compiler Fact 2: ALL source code files must be supplied in the compiler command for it to link and create an executable. If your source code is broken into 100 files, you need to compile all 100 together. The corrected split-main.cpp now includes the prototype: int sum(int a[], int n); before main(). The compiler checks argument types and usage of return value against the prototype. The compilation command lists both files: $ g++ -g split-main.cpp split-sum.cpp -o split, then $ ./split produces output 15.
notes_text: The prototype acts as a promise to the compiler that the function exists somewhere. The linker later verifies this promise by finding the actual definition. If no definition is found, a linker error (undefined reference) occurs. Always list every .cpp file in the compile command.

images.description: Code showing split-main.cpp with the added prototype 'int sum(int a[], int n);' highlighted, and split-sum.cpp with the function definition. A terminal shows successful compilation of both files and output of 15.

title: Undefined References
summary: Explains the 'undefined reference' linker error caused by forgetting to list source files or having prototype/definition mismatches, a very common error in CS 103/104.
main_text: Forgetting to list a source code file on the command line results in an 'undefined reference' error! These are quite common in CS 103 and CS 104 so please know their cause and what to look for to fix them. We must provide ALL .cpp (or later, .o) files that have relevant code for our application. Whenever you see an 'undefined reference', you've either: 1. (80% of the time) Forgot to list a source file on the g++ command line - verify all files are listed. 2. (20% of the time) Have a typo in the prototype or function definition - for example, prototyped int sum(char[], int) but defined int sum(int[], int). Examples: compiling only split-main.cpp produces 'undefined reference to sum(int*, int)'. Compiling only split-sum.cpp produces 'undefined reference to main'.
notes_text: Undefined reference errors come from the linker, not the compiler. They occur after compilation succeeds but the linker cannot find the actual function implementation. The error messages mention the mangled function signature, which can help identify prototype/definition mismatches.

images.description: A warning callout box listing the two causes of undefined reference errors with percentages (80% missing file, 20% typo). Two terminal windows show the error messages: one from compiling only split-main.cpp (undefined reference to sum) and one from compiling only split-sum.cpp (undefined reference to main).
labels: Forgot to list a source file
Have a typo in the prototype

title: Header Files
summary: Introduces header (.h) files as the solution for sharing function prototypes across multiple source files and applications, avoiding redundant prototype declarations.
main_text: Suppose split-sum.cpp defined multiple functions (i.e. more than just sum()). Further suppose other applications would like to use those functions. Rather than each application retyping the prototypes, place them in a header (.h) file and #include it into each source (.cpp) file that uses it. Header files will also be used to define classes (objects) in the future. The example shows split-sum.h containing just the prototype: int sum(int a[], int n);. The split-sum.cpp file includes its own header with #include "sum.h" and contains the implementation. Two different applications (split-main.cpp and other-app.cpp) both #include "split-sum.h" to access the sum function prototype, allowing them to call sum() without retyping the prototype.
notes_text: Header files are the standard mechanism in C++ for sharing interfaces between source files. The convention is to name the header file the same as the corresponding .cpp file but with a .h extension. Use angle brackets (#include <>) for system headers and quotes (#include "") for user-defined headers.

images.description: A diagram showing the relationship between header and source files: split-sum.h (containing the prototype) is included by both split-main.cpp and other-app.cpp via #include directives. split-sum.cpp also includes its own header. Yellow arrows show the include relationships.

title: Multifile Compilation - Easy as 1, 2, 3
summary: Provides a three-step recipe for multifile compilation: create header files with prototypes, create source files with implementations, and compile all .cpp files together.
main_text: Step 1: Create a header (.h) file and move the prototypes of the functions you will move to a separate file. #include that file in each .cpp that needs it. Example: split-sum.h contains the prototype int sum(int a[], int n);. Step 2: Create a source (.cpp) file and move the code of the functions you'd like to separate. Example: split-sum.cpp contains #include "split-sum.h" and the implementation of int sum(int a[], int n) with the for loop. Step 3: Compile ALL the .cpp files (NOT the header / .h files) together by listing all the .cpp files in the g++ command. Examples: $ g++ -g split-main.cpp split-sum.cpp -o split, or $ g++ -g other-app.cpp split-sum.cpp -o other-app.
notes_text: This three-step process is the standard workflow for organizing C++ projects. Note that .h files are never listed directly in the g++ command - they are automatically included when the preprocessor processes the #include directives in the .cpp files.

images.description: Code examples for each step: split-sum.h with prototype only, split-sum.cpp with #include and implementation, and terminal commands showing how to compile all .cpp files together for different applications.

title: Header File Dos and Don'ts
summary: Lists important rules for using header files: never compile .h files directly, always #include headers in .cpp files that use them, and recompile when headers change.
main_text: NEVER compile .h files in a g++ command. Simply compile the .cpp files and the #include'd header files will be compiled as part of those. DO #include header files in each source (.cpp) file that uses those functions (or, later, C++ classes). DO recompile any .cpp files that #include the header file WHEN the header file changes. The slide shows an incorrect command with a prohibition symbol: $ g++ -g split-sum.h split-main.cpp split-sum.cpp -o split (wrong - don't list .h files). The correct commands are: $ g++ -g split-main.cpp split-sum.cpp -o split and $ g++ -g other-app.cpp split-sum.cpp -o other-app.
notes_text: Including .h files on the g++ command line can cause unexpected behavior or duplicate symbol errors. The preprocessor handles .h files automatically through #include directives. When a header changes, all .cpp files that include it must be recompiled to pick up the changes - this is what build systems like Make automate.

images.description: Two terminal windows contrasting incorrect and correct compilation commands. The incorrect command lists a .h file and has a prohibition symbol overlay. The correct commands only list .cpp files.

title: Basic Debugging Section Header
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of content on basic debugging techniques for finding and fixing errors in C++ programs.
main_text: This is a section header slide with the heading BASIC DEBUGGING. It introduces the topic of debugging techniques that students can use to find and fix errors in their programs, including test cases, hand-tracing, print statements, and debugger tools.
notes_text: Debugging is a critical skill for programmers. This section covers a systematic three-step approach: creating test cases with expected outputs, hand-tracing code, and using print statements or debugger tools to locate bugs.

title: Bugs - The Original Bug
summary: Shows the historical origin of the term 'bug' in computing - a real moth found in a Harvard Mark II relay in 1947, the first documented computer bug.
main_text: This slide shows the original 'bug' - a historical photograph of the logbook entry from September 9, 1947, when operators of the Harvard Mark II computer found an actual moth trapped in Relay #70, Panel F. The handwritten entry reads 'First actual case of bug being found.' The moth was taped to the logbook page. This is considered the origin of the term 'bug' to describe computer errors, though the term was already in informal use before this incident. The logbook shows timestamps (0800, 1000, 1100, 1525, 1545) with notes about tests being run when the moth was discovered.
notes_text: While Grace Hopper is often credited with finding this bug, it was actually found by her team. The term 'bug' for technical glitches predates computers, but this incident popularized its use in computing. The original logbook is preserved at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.

images.description: A photograph of the original logbook page from September 9, 1947, showing handwritten entries with timestamps and a real moth (insect) taped to the page. The entry notes 'First actual case of bug being found' next to 'Relay #70 Panel F (moth) in relay.'
labels: First actual case of bug being found

title: Step 1: Test Cases and Expected Outputs
summary: Describes the first debugging step: working out correct expected outputs on paper before running the program, using binary search as an example.
main_text: Do a few examples on paper and work out what the correct (expected) outputs should be (both intermediate results and final results). You cannot effectively debug without an expectation of the right output so you know when the program is working. Example: For binary search, take the input array and target value and show how start and end will update on each iteration. The slide shows a binary search example with tgt = 12 on the sorted list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 19] at indices 0-8. The trace shows: start=0, i=4, end=8; then start=4, i=6, end=8; then start=4, i=5, end=6; then start=5, end=6; then start=5, end=5 (converged but not found, since 12 is not in the list).
notes_text: Working out expected outputs by hand is the most important debugging step. Without knowing what the correct answer should be, you cannot identify when your program produces wrong results. This applies to both final outputs and intermediate variable values at each step of the algorithm.

images.description: A series of array diagrams showing binary search iterations on the list [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19] searching for target 12. Each iteration shows the array with start, i (mid), and end pointers moving closer together, demonstrating how to manually trace the algorithm's behavior.

title: Step 2: Hand-Tracing
summary: Explains hand-tracing as a debugging technique where you manually trace code execution line by line, tracking variable values in a table and comparing to expected outputs.
main_text: Use one of your input scenarios that is not working and trace the execution of your code by hand. Make a table of variables and walk the code line by line. Compare to the expected values from Step 1. The slide shows a binary search function (bsearch) with parameters list[], len, and tgt. The code initializes start = 0, end = len, then loops while start != end, computing mid = (start + end) / 2, checking if tgt equals list[mid] (return mid), if tgt > list[mid] (start = mid), or else (end = mid). The example uses len=9, tgt=12 on the list [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19]. A table with columns for start, end, and mid is provided (empty) for students to fill in as they trace through the code.
notes_text: Hand-tracing is where you become the computer. This technique reveals bugs by showing exactly where actual variable values diverge from expected values. The empty table format encourages systematic tracking. This particular binary search implementation has a bug (start = mid instead of start = mid + 1) which the hand trace will reveal.

images.description: An array diagram showing the initial state of binary search with start at index 0, mid at index 4, and end at index 9 (past the array). Below is the bsearch function code and an empty table with columns for start, end, and mid to be filled during hand-tracing.

title: Step 3: Print Statements / Narration
summary: Introduces using print statements as a debugging technique to let the computer trace execution for you, narrating where the program is and what variable values are.
main_text: Let the computer 'trace' for you by using print statements. Now that you know what to expect, the most common and easy way to find the error is to add print statements that will 'narrate' where you are and what the variable values are. Be a detective by narrowing down where the error is. Put a print statement in each 'for', 'while', 'if' or 'else' block... this will make sure you are getting to the expected areas of your code. Then print variable values so you can see what data your program is producing.
notes_text: Print statement debugging (also called printf debugging or narration) is the most accessible debugging technique. The key insight is to print not just variable values but also location indicators (which branch was taken, which iteration of a loop) to build a complete picture of program execution flow.

images.description: A cartoon detective with a magnifying glass, representing the investigative nature of debugging.

title: Example of Print Statements
summary: Contrasts novice print statements (printing only variable values) with quality print statements that include context labels, showing both approaches side by side.
main_text: This slide compares novice and quality print statements in a binary search function. The novice version (shown on red/pink background) adds only: cout << "mid " << mid << endl; inside the while loop - printing just the mid value with no context. The quality version (shown on green background) adds comprehensive narration: cout << "Starting bsearch: len=" << len << " and target=" << tgt << endl; at the start, then inside the loop: cout << "New iter: start=" << start << " and end=" << end << endl; followed by cout << "\tChecking mid=" << mid << endl; and cout << "\tdata=" << list[mid] << endl;. Each branch prints its decision: cout << "Found!" << endl;, cout << "\tLarger half" << endl;, or cout << "\tSmaller half" << endl;. The tab characters (\t) provide indentation for readability.
notes_text: Quality print statements include three elements: (1) a label identifying where in the code the print occurs, (2) the values of relevant variables, and (3) which branch or decision was taken. The tab character \t helps visually group related output. This level of detail makes it much easier to compare actual execution with expected behavior.

images.description: Side-by-side code comparison: left side (red background) shows binary search with a single minimal print statement, right side (green background) shows the same function with comprehensive, labeled print statements at every decision point.

title: Which Debug Output is Most Helpful?
summary: Compares the actual runtime output of novice vs quality print statements, showing the quality version reveals the infinite loop bug through clear iteration tracking.
main_text: This slide shows the actual terminal output from running the binary search with both print statement approaches searching for target 12 in the list [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19]. The novice output (left terminal) shows: $ ./bsearch followed by mid 4, mid 6, mid 5, mid 5, mid 5, mid 5, mid 5... repeating infinitely. This reveals an infinite loop but gives little information about why. The quality output (right terminal) shows: Starting bsearch: len=9 and target=12, New iter: start=0 and end=9, Checking mid=4, data=9, Larger half, New iter: start=4 and end=9, Checking mid=6, data=13, Smaller half, New iter: start=4 and end=6, Checking mid=5, data=11, Larger half, New iter: start=5 and end=6, Checking mid=5, data=11, Larger half... The quality output clearly shows that start=5 never advances past 5 because start = mid sets start to 5 when mid is already 5, revealing the bug.
notes_text: The quality output makes the bug obvious: when start=5 and end=6, mid=(5+6)/2=5, and setting start=mid keeps start at 5, creating an infinite loop. The fix is start = mid + 1. This example powerfully demonstrates why descriptive print statements are worth the extra typing effort.

images.description: Left side shows array diagrams tracing the binary search iterations with start, i, and end pointers converging but getting stuck. Two terminal windows compare output: left shows repetitive 'mid 5' (novice), right shows detailed iteration info including start, end, mid, data values, and branch decisions (quality).

title: Fixed Code
summary: Shows the corrected binary search code with the bug fix: changing 'start = mid' to 'start = mid+1' to prevent the infinite loop.
main_text: This slide shows the fixed binary search code with quality print statements retained. The function int bsearch(int list[], int len, int tgt) initializes start = 0, end = len, and loops while start != end. Inside the loop, it prints iteration info: cout << "New iter: start=" << start << " and end=" << end << endl;, computes mid = (start + end) / 2, prints the mid index and data value being checked. If tgt == list[mid], it prints "Found!" and returns mid. If tgt > list[mid], it prints "Larger half" and executes the fix: start = mid+1 (highlighted in yellow, changed from the buggy start = mid). Otherwise it prints "Smaller half" and sets end = mid. If the loop exits, it returns -1. The key fix is start = mid+1 which ensures start always advances, preventing the infinite loop when mid equals start.
notes_text: The fix (start = mid + 1) is a classic binary search correction. When searching the larger half, the mid element has already been checked, so start should skip past it. Without the +1, when end - start equals 1, mid equals start due to integer division, causing start = mid to never change, creating an infinite loop.

images.description: The complete fixed binary search function code on a green background with quality print statements. The line 'start = mid+1;' is highlighted in yellow to emphasize the bug fix.

title: Meta-Idea: Binary Search for Debugging
summary: Introduces the concept of using a binary search approach to locate bugs in code by inserting print statements at midpoints to narrow down the error location.
main_text: Think of debugging as performing a 'binary search' for the bug/error. If the program crashes and you aren't sure where, or a variable has an unexpected value, add print statements at the mid-point and see if things are still good there. If not, the error is in the first half of the code. Otherwise, the error is in the second half of the code. Repeat the process on that half. The slide demonstrates with an example: a program prog.cpp that gets a Segmentation fault when run. First, add a print statement at line 50 (the midpoint): cout << "L50 x:" << x << endl;. Running shows L50 x:42 followed by Segmentation fault, meaning the code up to line 50 is OK but the error is between lines 50 and the end. The error region is then narrowed to between lines 50 and 60, and further bisection continues until the exact bug line is found.
notes_text: This meta-strategy applies the binary search algorithm concept to the debugging process itself. Instead of reading every line of code, you can efficiently locate a bug in O(log n) steps where n is the number of lines. This is especially valuable for segmentation faults and crashes where the error location is completely unknown.

Right shows the same program with a print statement inserted at line 50, revealing the crash occurs after line 50. Below, the code is annotated showing the OK region and Error region separated by the print statement.

title: More Tips - Incremental Development
summary: Presents incremental development as a strategy: write small portions, compile and test frequently, add features one at a time, and comment out code to isolate problems.
main_text: 1. Don't write the entire program all at once. 2. Write a small portion, compile and test it. Write the code to get the input values, add some couts to print out what you got from the user, and make sure it is what you expect. Write a single loop and test it before doing nested loops. 3. Once one part works, add another part and test it. 4. Comment out later portions of the code and verify earlier parts work and then add your later code back in little-by-little to find where it stops/starts working.
notes_text: Incremental development is a fundamental software engineering practice that reduces debugging difficulty by keeping the amount of untested code small at any time. Each small addition is verified before moving on, making it easy to identify which change introduced a bug. This approach also builds confidence in the correctness of earlier code.

title: Alternative to Step 3 - Using a Debugger Tool
summary: Briefly introduces debugger tools as an alternative to print statements for examining program execution, with more coverage promised in lab.
main_text: Use a debugger tool as an alternative to Step 3 (print statements). A debugger is a program that allows you to see inside and slow down your program so you can understand what it is doing (vs. what you expect it to do). More details and hands-on practice will be covered in lab. Debugger tools like gdb allow you to set breakpoints, step through code line by line, inspect variable values, and examine the call stack without modifying your source code with print statements.
notes_text: Debuggers are more powerful than print statements because they let you pause execution at any point, inspect any variable, and step through code without modifying the source. The -g flag in the g++ command enables debugger support by embedding debugging symbols in the executable. Common debuggers include gdb (command line) and its GUI frontparts like kdbg.
